title: The scout
hookLine: a long portrait of the Cynic as scout and witness, sent to report what's really good
last: SOMEONE YOU CAN LIVE WITH IS THERE.

cards: Before an ancient army moved, it sent a few people ahead. They slipped into the hills, looked at the ground, counted the campfires across the valley, and came back to say what was really there.
Everything hung on that report. A scout who panicked and said a thousand enemies when there were ten could send a whole army running from nothing. Epictetus loved this picture.
In one of the longest talks in the Discourses, book three, chapter twenty-two, he uses it to describe a certain kind of philosopher.

teach.h: THE CYNICS: NAMED FOR THE DOG.
teach.b: First, the Cynics: a Greek movement usually traced back more than four centuries before Epictetus, to Diogenes of Sinope, who lived on almost nothing: a rough cloak, a bag, a staff, and a large storage jar to sleep in.
Their name most likely comes from kyon, Greek for dog. It seems to have started as an insult, and they wore it on purpose. Then the scout.

teach.h: SENT AHEAD TO SEE WHAT IS GOOD.
teach.b: The true Cynic, Epictetus says, is sent ahead to find out what is friendly to human beings and what is hostile, and to come back and report it truthfully. Not frightened or dazzled into a false one.
The report: people hunt for happiness where it isn't, in money, office and others' good opinion, and it lives in their own choices.
Most of that long chapter is a warning. A young man asks about taking up the Cynic life, and Epictetus tells him, in effect, don't you dare do it lightly. The cloak and staff are the easy part.
The real Cynic has nothing to hide, keeps his mind clean, takes a beating without hating the one who gives it, and cares for everyone like a father or a brother.
In book one, Epictetus says Diogenes was sent out as a scout and came back with a calm report: death is no evil, because it isn't shameful.
Elsewhere he calls the philosopher a witness, whose own life shows you can lose what the world prizes and still be well. You don't need a cloak for the small version.
A scout simply looks at what's there and says so.

how: People who practice Stoicism often try to separate what happened from what they added to it, and to describe events to others plainly, the way Epictetus' scout reports the ground.

games.q: you're the scout. from the ridge the enemy camp looks enormous, but you count only ten fires. what do you report?
o: a huge army: better safe than sorry.
ten fires, exactly what you saw.
nothing until someone else confirms it.
games.why: Epictetus' scout reports what is really there, not what fear adds. a frightened report can send a whole army running from nothing.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you'll report on today, how a meeting went, how a parent sounded on the phone, and notice the report you'd usually give, shaped by worry or by wanting to look good.
Then ask slowly: what did I actually see, and what did I add? Hold only the plain report, the ten fires, no more and no less.

wordCard.voice: The scout. Epictetus' picture of the philosopher sent ahead to see what is truly good and bad, and to come back and report it honestly, without fear. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: a scout or spy, one who looks things over; Epictetus' word for the Cynic sent ahead.

carryVoice: Your line: a scout. Report what you saw, with nothing added and nothing hidden. Until tomorrow.
